1	\section{Analysis}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
5	\label{sec:heterogeneity}
6	
7	The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
8	We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
9	High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.
10	
11	Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
12	The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.
13	
14	Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
15	Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp
16	
17	Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
18	The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
19	Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
20	Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
21	The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
22	This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.
23	
24	In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling
25	
26	The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
27	Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
28	Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

58	
59	\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
60	\label{sec:diagnostic}
61	
62	The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
63	This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:
64	
65	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
66	\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
67	\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
68	\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
69	  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
70	  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
71	  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
72	  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.38$): counterproductive.
73	  \end{itemize}
74	\end{enumerate}
75	
76	Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
77	Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
78	The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.

3	\section{Aggressive Compression}
4	\label{sec:aggressive}
5	
6	At $4\times$ compression, Llama and Mistral show minimal benefit from non-uniform allocation.
7	At more aggressive ratios, the picture changes: at $5.3\times$ (average 3 bits), constrained MCKP achieves $45\times$ lower PPL than uniform on Llama (57.60 vs.\ 2643.77) and $44\times$ on Mistral (11.91 vs.\ 519.11), because the constraint protects sensitive heads from 2-bit assignment.
8	At $8\times$, the budget is too constrained for any allocation to preserve quality (both methods degrade catastrophically).
9	The intermediate regime ($5.3\times$) provides the largest relative benefit.
10	
11	\section{Profiling Resolution and Stability}
12	\label{sec:profiling_resolution}
13	
14	We compare standard-resolution profiling (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) against high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens) on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression.
15	
16	High-resolution profiling improves constrained MCKP from 11.23 to 10.91 PPL ($-$0.32 absolute).
17	Relative to the bf16 baseline (9.81), this reduces the degradation from 1.42 to 1.10, a 22.5\% reduction.
18	The improvement comes from finer-grained sensitivity estimates: standard profiling detects non-zero 2-bit distortion in 37 of 112 heads, while high-resolution profiling detects 100 of 112 (2.7$\times$ more).
19	
20	The additional signal changes 8 of 112 head assignments.
21	High-resolution profiling protects shallow layers (L1--L3) at higher bit-widths while compressing mid-layers (L5--L11) more aggressively---a redistribution that standard profiling misses because its distortion estimates for these heads fall below the noise floor.
22	
23	\paragraph{Multi-seed stability.}
24	The profiled allocation is stable across calibration subsets.
25	Under hires profiling on Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL $10.99 \pm 0.06$ across 3 random calibration seeds (individual runs: 11.02, 10.90, 11.05), with std/mean below 0.6\%.
26	The bit distribution is identical across all seeds ($\{$2-bit: 8, 4-bit: 100, 8-bit: 4$\}$), and 101 of 112 heads (90.2\%) receive the same assignment in all three runs.
27	This stability confirms that the per-head sensitivity ranking is robust to calibration sampling noise.
28	
29	\paragraph{Numerical precision.}
30	Float32 profiling (64 $\times$ 2048 tokens) yields an identical constrained allocation and PPL within seed variance (10.89 vs.\ 10.91, $\Delta = 0.02 < \sigma = 0.06$), confirming that bfloat16 precision is sufficient for the profiling step.
31	
32	\paragraph{Per-layer optimality.}
33	To validate the additive distortion assumption underlying the MCKP formulation, we compare constrained MCKP against a per-layer brute-force oracle that exhaustively enumerates all $4^4 = 256$ bit-width combinations within each 4-head group on Qwen2.5-7B (hires profiling).
34	Of the 8 layers admitting multiple feasible allocations, MCKP matches the oracle exactly in 5; the remaining 3 show gaps of 0.018 (Layer~1), 0.014 (Layer~11), and 0.005 (Layer~4) PPL.
35	All three gaps involve repositioning a 2-bit assignment among heads with near-identical sensitivity within the same layer bit budget.
36	The negligible total gap ($<0.04$ PPL) confirms that the per-head additive distortion model closely approximates the true layer-level interaction.
37	
38	\section{KV Separation Ablation}
39	\label{sec:kv_separation}
40	
41	We test whether treating K and V caches as independent items in the MCKP solver---allowing different bit-widths for K and V within the same head---improves over joint allocation where K and V share a bit-width.
42	
43	Joint allocation achieves 10.91 PPL; separated K/V allocation achieves 11.22 ($+$0.31 worse).
44	The degradation stems from K-side over-compression: the separated solver doubles the maximum number of 2-bit K items to 16 (vs.\ 8 in the joint formulation), since K and V are counted independently against the cardinality constraint.
45	Meanwhile, V-side distortion is near-zero for most heads, so the solver assigns all V items to 4-bit, concentrating compression entirely on K.
46	
47	Of the 112 heads, 21 show K$\neq$V asymmetry in the separated allocation, all with K receiving a lower bit-width than V.
48	This systematic asymmetry suggests that K caches are inherently more compressible than V caches, consistent with the observation that key vectors primarily encode positional information while value vectors carry content.
49	
50	Joint allocation is sufficient under the current constraint formulation.
51	Separated K/V allocation with per-side cardinality constraints---limiting 2-bit assignments independently for K and V---is a direction for future work.
52	
53	\section{Runtime Benchmark}
54	\label{sec:runtime}
55	
56	\begin{table}[h]
57	\centering
58	\caption{PyTorch-level latency on Qwen2.5-7B (single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB), prompt\_len=256, gen\_len=128, mean of 10 runs). All conditions store KV in bf16 with simulated per-head quantize/dequantize calls; peak GPU memory is identical across rows.}
59	\label{tab:runtime}
60	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
61	\toprule
62	Condition & Prefill (ms) & Decode (ms/tok) & Throughput (tok/s) \\
63	\midrule
64	Baseline bf16       & 45.86 & 33.78 & 29.6 \\
65	Uniform 4-bit       & 54.25 & 42.46 & 23.6 \\
66	Constrained MCKP    & 57.03 & 46.09 & 21.8 \\
67	\bottomrule
68	\end{tabular}
69	\end{table}
70	
71	Table~\ref{tab:runtime} reports end-to-end latency for three KV cache configurations.
72	Uniform 4-bit quantization adds 25.7\% decode overhead relative to the bf16 baseline (42.46 vs.\ 33.78~ms/tok), reflecting per-head quantize/dequantize calls at every attention step.
73	Constrained MCKP adds a further 8.5\% over uniform (46.09 vs.\ 42.46~ms/tok), because mixed-precision allocation dispatches different dequantization kernels for 2-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit heads within the same layer.
74	The MCKP solver itself runs in ${\sim}5$~ms and is invoked once at initialization, contributing negligibly to end-to-end latency.
75	Both quantized conditions achieve the same $4\times$ KV cache compression (5.25~MB vs.\ 21~MB at bf16), so the latency difference between uniform and MCKP reflects only the mixed-precision dispatch overhead, not a memory trade-off.
76	
77	\paragraph{Caveat.}
78	These measurements use PyTorch-level per-head \texttt{quantize}/\texttt{dequantize} calls and do \emph{not} represent optimized CUDA kernel performance.
79	Production inference engines such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM employ fused attention kernels that batch dequantization with the matrix multiply, amortizing the per-head dispatch cost that dominates the gap between uniform and MCKP in our simulation.
80	The 8.5\% overhead reported here should therefore be treated as an upper bound on the mixed-precision penalty; real-world deployment with fused kernels would likely narrow or eliminate this gap.
81	The limitation noted in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}---that we report no real-kernel latency benchmarks---remains: the numbers above quantify simulation overhead, not production inference speedup.

59	\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
60	\label{sec:diagnostic}
61	
62	The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
63	This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:
64	
65	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
66	\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
67	\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
68	\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
69	  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
70	  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
71	  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
72	  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.38$): counterproductive.
73	  \end{itemize}
74	\end{enumerate}
75	
76	Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
77	Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
78	The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
79	Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
80	The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
81	
82	\subsection{Granularity Tradeoff}
83	\label{sec:granularity}
84	
85	Quantization budget can in principle be allocated at three granularities, each with a distinct cost--benefit profile.
86	\emph{Layer-level} allocation (KVmix~\cite{li2025kvmix}, KVTuner~\cite{li2025kvtuner}) keeps the search space small ($L$ layers) but forces all heads in a layer to share one bitwidth.
87	This is fundamentally limited when within-layer variance is large: in Qwen2.5-7B Layer-0, per-head 2-bit deltas are 6.74, 2.12, 1.31, and 1.24---a more than $5\times$ spread that any layer-level assignment must average over.
88	\emph{Per-head} allocation (ours) exposes this heterogeneity to the solver and yields a 27.3\% PPL improvement on Qwen, at the cost of $H$ profiling passes; the cardinality constraint developed in \S\ref{sec:cardinality} renders the choice of solver irrelevant, amortizing the search overhead.
89	\emph{Token-level} allocation (ZipCache~\cite{he2024zipcache}, KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi}) is the finest grain available but introduces runtime overhead from online importance scoring.
90	Importantly, per-head and per-token granularities are orthogonal: a head's bitwidth (static, determined offline) and a token's importance (dynamic, determined online) compose without conflict, so the two can be combined.
91	Per-head therefore occupies the sweet spot for static allocation---fine enough to capture the head-level heterogeneity that drives MCKP benefit on spread architectures, yet free of any per-step runtime cost.
92	
93	Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.
94

\subsection{Granularity Tradeoff}
\label{sec:granularity}

Quantization budget can in principle be allocated at three granularities, each with a distinct cost--benefit profile.
\emph{Layer-level} allocation (KVmix~\cite{li2025kvmix}, KVTuner~\cite{li2025kvtuner}) keeps the search space small ($L$ layers) but forces all heads in a layer to share one bitwidth.
This is fundamentally limited when within-layer variance is large: in Qwen2.5-7B Layer-0, per-head 2-bit deltas are 6.74, 2.12, 1.31, and 1.24---a more than $5\times$ spread that any layer-level assignment must average over.
\emph{Per-head} allocation (ours) exposes this heterogeneity to the solver and yields a 27.3\% PPL improvement on Qwen, at the cost of $H$ profiling passes; the cardinality constraint developed in \S\ref{sec:cardinality} renders the choice of solver irrelevant, amortizing the search overhead.
\emph{Token-level} allocation (ZipCache~\cite{he2024zipcache}, KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi}) is the finest grain available but introduces runtime overhead from online importance scoring.
Importantly, per-head and per-token granularities are orthogonal: a head's bitwidth (static, determined offline) and a token's importance (dynamic, determined online) compose without conflict, so the two can be combined.
Per-head therefore occupies the sweet spot for static allocation---fine enough to capture the head-level heterogeneity that drives MCKP benefit on spread architectures, yet free of any per-step runtime cost.

Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

MCKP outperforms both heuristics, but the best non-uniform result (7.16) still exceeds uniform by 0.03 PPL, reinforcing that non-uniform allocation is counterproductive when heterogeneity is low.
Note that the heuristic baselines use a slightly higher budget (0.256 vs.\ 0.248 for MCKP, a 3\% difference) because integer $k$ does not divide evenly into the target; despite this advantage, they still underperform MCKP, making the comparison conservative.

\label{sec:downstream}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{0-shot accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B at 4$\times$ compression. Constrained MCKP recovers approximately 73\% of the accuracy lost by uniform 4-bit quantization.}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Task & Baseline & Uniform & MCKP & $\Delta$ vs \\

\midrule

HellaSwag  & ---   & 0.728 & 0.768 & $+$4.0 pts \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:downstream} shows that the PPL improvements transfer to downstream tasks on Qwen2.5-7B.
Constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 points over uniform 4-bit (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), with gains on all four benchmarks.
The largest gain appears on HellaSwag ($+$4.0 pts), where language modeling quality is most directly reflected.

Constrained MCKP recovers approximately 73\% of the accuracy lost by uniform 4-bit quantization, indicating that per-head bit allocation addresses much of the degradation, though a gap to bf16 remains.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Stability}
\label{sec:cross_dataset}

To verify that the profiled allocation is not overfit to the calibration corpus, we profile on C4 and evaluate on WikiText-2, and vice versa, at $4\times$ compression.
On Qwen2.5-7B, C4-calibrated MCKP achieves 11.29 PPL on WikiText-2 (vs.\ 15.45 uniform, a 27\% reduction), only 0.06 PPL above the WikiText-2-calibrated result (11.23).

Whether non-uniform allocation helps is determined by the model's intrinsic head sensitivity heterogeneity, not the calibration data.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the objective's additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors are large enough to compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL for these allocations; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher.
At 4-bit and above, per-head distortions are small and compound negligibly---uniform 4-bit achieves close to its additive prediction---but 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger.
When most heads are quantized to 2-bit simultaneously, cumulative truncation errors exceed the network's capacity to compensate, and perplexity degrades super-linearly.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.

A surprising consequence is that, under the cardinality constraint, the choice of solver becomes irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical allocations---not approximately, but exactly: all 112 heads receive the same bit-width on Qwen2.5-7B, all 256 on Llama-3.1-8B, and 255 of 256 on Mistral-7B-v0.3 (the single difference is a zero-distortion tie with no PPL impact).
The constraint narrows the feasible set enough that greedy's locally optimal decisions are globally optimal (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm without sacrificing solution quality.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap across 28 layers is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On Llama-3.1-8B, constrained MCKP achieves 8.45 PPL vs.\ uniform 8.47---essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
On Mistral-7B-v0.3, it is slightly \emph{worse}: 7.16 vs.\ 7.13.
On Yi-1.5-9B, non-uniform allocation provides no benefit (7.22 vs.\ 7.22 uniform) despite Yi-1.5 having the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1).
On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1, the lowest ratio tested), degradation is 0.3\% (9.05 vs.\ 9.03).
The difference across architectures traces to head sensitivity heterogeneity---specifically, its \emph{distribution shape}, not GQA ratio alone.
Qwen's KV heads vary widely in 2-bit distortion, with Layer-0 heads forming a cluster of high sensitivity; Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier but otherwise uniform heads (a ``spike'' pattern that MCKP cannot exploit); Gemma-2 and Mistral show near-uniform sensitivity across all heads.
When there is no exploitable heterogeneity, non-uniform allocation adds noise without benefit.

This motivates a diagnostic question that prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint heterogeneity diagnostic based on concentration \emph{and} distribution shape of per-head distortion (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
On our five architectures, the diagnostic separates the beneficial case (Qwen, concentration 0.61, spread pattern) from cases where non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen's, but its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike with no cross-bitwidth gradient---precisely the pattern where MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
The diagnostic reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no computational overhead.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint makes solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent per-head allocations across three architectures, enabling use of a simple greedy algorithm (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates architectures where non-uniform allocation helps from those where it does not, across all five models tested. Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{KV Cache Quantization.}
4	Uniform-precision methods quantize the KV cache at a single bit-width across all heads, using techniques such as asymmetric per-channel/per-token schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant}, quantization--serving co-design~\cite{lin2024qserve}, salient-token identification~\cite{he2024zipcache}, low-rank plus sparse correction~\cite{kang2024gear}, sliding-window adaptation~\cite{duanmu2024skvq}, rotation-based outlier smoothing for robust 2-bit~\cite{su2025rotatekv}, 2-bit with adaptive token retention~\cite{sharma2025minikv}, and adapter-based inter-layer prediction at 2--2.5 bits~\cite{shutova2025aquakv}.
5	We extend the design space to per-head non-uniform allocation over hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$.
6	
7	\paragraph{KV Cache Eviction.}
8	Complementary to quantization, eviction methods reduce cache size by discarding tokens---retaining heavy-hitters~\cite{zhang2023h2o}, per-head important tokens~\cite{li2024snapkv,ge2024fastgen}, persistent-importance tokens~\cite{liu2024scissorhands}, attention sinks~\cite{xiao2024streamingllm}, or progressively fewer tokens in deeper layers~\cite{yang2024pyramidinfer}.
9	Recent per-head eviction methods allocate non-uniform budgets across heads based on retrieval-vs-reasoning importance~\cite{fu2025headkv} or adaptive optimization extending SnapKV/PyramidKV~\cite{feng2025adakv}, confirming that head-level heterogeneity is exploitable for eviction; our work shows it is equally exploitable for quantization.
10	
11	
12	\paragraph{Mixed-Precision Quantization (Weights).}
13	Mixed-precision allocation has a long history at the weight level.
14	HAWQ~\cite{dong2019hawq} and HAWQ-V2~\cite{dong2020hawqv2} use second-order (Hessian-based) sensitivity to assign per-layer bit-widths, with V2 introducing block-wise trace-weighted scoring and Pareto-frontier selection; HAQ~\cite{wang2019haq} learns an allocation by reinforcement learning under hardware-aware latency/energy constraints.
15	These methods establish that non-uniform bit-width allocation is effective when per-component sensitivity is heterogeneous; we transfer this insight from weights to the KV cache at per-head granularity, where heterogeneity is empirically much larger (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
16	
17	\paragraph{Mixed-Precision Rate-Distortion Allocation.}
18	RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formulates per-head bit-width selection as an MCKP and proves greedy optimality for consecutive bit-widths $\{2,\ldots,6\}$ via the polymatroid structure, which relies on the assumption that per-head distortions decompose additively into the global objective---valid when adjacent bit-widths differ by a single bit so that quantization noise stays in the small-perturbation regime.
19	On hardware-aligned $\{2,4,8,16\}$, the 4$\times$ gap between 2-bit and 4-bit drives 2-bit distortion to compound super-additively, breaking the polymatroid structure and the additivity assumption with it.
20	Concretely, running RateQuant's greedy algorithm (Algorithm~1) directly on $\{2,4,8,16\}$ yields 32.45 PPL on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression---catastrophically worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45)---whereas our cardinality constraint on simultaneously active 2-bit heads recovers 11.23 PPL at the same average bit-width (Table~\ref{tab:solver_equiv}).
21	The constraint is the minimal fix that restores the additive regime in which RateQuant's polymatroid argument applies.
22	Related mixed-precision KV-cache work operates at coarser granularity---layer-level via gradient-based sensitivity~\cite{li2025kvmix} or Pareto search over hardware-friendly precision pairs~\cite{li2025kvtuner}, block-level via progressive decoding-step quantization for long-CoT reasoning~\cite{liu2025pmkvq}, channel-level via dynamic precision boost on sensitive Key channels~\cite{xia2025kitty}, token-level via a learned on-device controller~\cite{haeriboroujeni2026dontwaste}, memory-budget-level~\cite{lei2026arkv}---at the weight level~\cite{kim2024squeezellm}, or dynamically at inference time~\cite{zhang2025mixkvq}; our allocation is static and per-head.
23	
24	\paragraph{Attention Head Analysis.}
25	Prior work studies head redundancy and pruning~\cite{voita2019analyzing,michel2019sixteen}, focusing on which heads can be removed entirely.
26	Our analysis asks a different question: which heads are sensitive to \emph{quantization}, and how heterogeneous that sensitivity is across architectures---a property that determines whether non-uniform allocation is beneficial (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate on five architectures spanning different grouped-query attention (GQA) configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA ratio 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112 KV heads),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192 KV heads),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads, sliding window attention),
and \textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336 KV heads, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 2:1 to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, and softcapped attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
We use two profiling resolutions: \emph{standard} (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) and \emph{high-resolution} (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens), both from WikiText-2 train.
Unless marked with $\dagger$, all results use standard-resolution profiling; Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} analyzes the effect of resolution.

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{PPL ($\downarrow$) on WikiText-2 at 4$\times$ compression. Unconstrained failure severity tracks heterogeneity shape: catastrophic on Qwen ($3.3\times$ bf16), moderate on Gemma-2 ($1.5\times$), near-benign on the remaining three (${\sim}1.1\times$). Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok). $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). $^*$BOS-corrected.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & Uncons. & Ours \\
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{11.23} \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$       & 7.02  & 7.22  & 7.56  & 7.22 \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$    & 8.09  & 8.47  & 8.63  & \textbf{8.45} \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 7.04  & 7.13  & 7.57  & 7.16$^\ddagger$ \\
Gemma-2-9B$^{*\dagger}$   & 6.02  & 6.15  & 8.85  & 6.17 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} summarizes the main results.
On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 11.23 PPL, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Higher-resolution profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok) further improves this to 10.91; we report the standard-profiling result here and analyze the effect of profiling resolution in Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.
Without the cardinality constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure caused by excessive 2-bit assignments that compound across layers.
The constraint eliminates this failure mode entirely.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 (std is 1.3\% of the uniform gap), with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%).
This is a genuine negative result: the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads, meaning the optimization has no reliable signal to exploit.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity by limiting head-level variation in effective context length.

On Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) achieves 7.22 PPL, essentially identical to uniform 7.22 ($<$0.01\% difference).
Despite having the highest GQA ratio in our evaluation (8:1) and the highest concentration tested (0.71), Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier (Layer-4 Head-3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern that leaves no cross-bitwidth gradient for the solver to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 9.05 PPL vs.\ uniform 9.03---a 0.3\% degradation.
Gemma-2 has the most uniform head sensitivity distribution across its 336 KV heads, consistent with its low GQA ratio and attention logit softcapping.

Unconstrained results for Llama, Mistral, Yi-1.5, and Gemma-2 are omitted (---) as those experiments were conducted only on Qwen, where the failure mode is most pronounced.
Figure~\ref{fig:allocation} visualizes the bit-width allocation on Qwen, showing how constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit while selectively assigning only the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.

\begin{figure}[t]

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Stability}
\label{sec:cross_dataset}

To verify that the profiled allocation is not overfit to the calibration corpus, we profile on C4 and evaluate on WikiText-2, and vice versa, at $4\times$ compression.
On Qwen2.5-7B, C4-calibrated MCKP achieves 11.29 PPL on WikiText-2 (vs.\ 15.45 uniform, a 27\% reduction), only 0.06 PPL above the WikiText-2-calibrated result (11.23).
In the reverse direction, WikiText-2-calibrated MCKP achieves 20.56 PPL on the C4 held-out split (vs.\ 35.42 uniform, a 42\% reduction; C4 bf16 baseline on this split is 15.32).
All three models show ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement across calibration sources: Qwen 96.4\% (108/112 heads), Llama 97.7\% (250/256), and Mistral 96.5\% (247/256).
Qwen's agreement is the most informative, as all 112 heads have variable assignments; on Llama, 253 of 256 heads are forced to 4-bit by the $k{=}2$ constraint, inflating agreement.
The cross-dataset results reinforce the heterogeneity-driven narrative: on Qwen, the MCKP benefit is preserved across calibration sources; on Llama and Mistral, the lack of benefit is equally stable---Llama's C4-calibrated MCKP is 0.18 PPL worse than uniform, and Mistral shows similar degradation ($-$0.03 to $-$0.05 PPL).
Whether non-uniform allocation helps is determined by the model's intrinsic head sensitivity heterogeneity, not the calibration data.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.38$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.

\subsection{Granularity Tradeoff}
\label{sec:granularity}

Quantization budget can in principle be allocated at three granularities, each with a distinct cost--benefit profile.
\emph{Layer-level} allocation (KVmix~\cite{li2025kvmix}, KVTuner~\cite{li2025kvtuner}) keeps the search space small ($L$ layers) but forces all heads in a layer to share one bitwidth.
This is fundamentally limited when within-layer variance is large: in Qwen2.5-7B Layer-0, per-head 2-bit deltas are 6.74, 2.12, 1.31, and 1.24---a more than $5\times$ spread that any layer-level assignment must average over.
\emph{Per-head} allocation (ours) exposes this heterogeneity to the solver and yields a 27.3\% PPL improvement on Qwen, at the cost of $H$ profiling passes; the cardinality constraint developed in \S\ref{sec:cardinality} renders the choice of solver irrelevant, amortizing the search overhead.
\emph{Token-level} allocation (ZipCache~\cite{he2024zipcache}, KIVI~\cite{liu2024kivi}) is the finest grain available but introduces runtime overhead from online importance scoring.
Importantly, per-head and per-token granularities are orthogonal: a head's bitwidth (static, determined offline) and a token's importance (dynamic, determined online) compose without conflict, so the two can be combined.
Per-head therefore occupies the sweet spot for static allocation---fine enough to capture the head-level heterogeneity that drives MCKP benefit on spread architectures, yet free of any per-step runtime cost.

Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:formulation}

We formulate per-head KV cache quantization as a constrained optimization problem.
Let $h \in \{1,\ldots,H\}$ index the KV heads across all layers, $b_h \in \mathcal{B}$ the bit-width assigned to head $h$, and $\mathcal{B} = \{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ the set of hardware-aligned bit-widths.
Each head $h$ has a profiled distortion function $d_h(b)$, the PPL increase when head $h$ is quantized to $b$ bits.
Given a memory budget ratio $R$ (e.g., $R = 0.25$ for $4\times$ compression), we seek the allocation that minimizes total distortion:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:objective}
\min_{\{b_h\}} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_h(b_h) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \frac{1}{H \cdot 16}\sum_{h=1}^{H} b_h \leq R.
\end{equation}

This is a multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP): each head selects one bit-width from $\mathcal{B}$ to minimize total distortion under a budget.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} solves this for consecutive bit-widths $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, where the polymatroid structure of the feasible set guarantees that greedy allocation is optimal (their Proposition 6).
Hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ are non-consecutive; the gaps break this structure, and greedy is no longer guaranteed to match the MCKP optimum.
Moreover, as we show in \S\ref{sec:compounding}, the objective itself is not well-behaved: distortions from 2-bit heads compound non-additively, making unconstrained optimization unreliable.

\subsection{PPL-based Per-Head Profiling}
\label{sec:profiling}

We profile each KV head independently by quantizing it to each $b \in \mathcal{B}$ while keeping all other heads at bf16, and measuring the resulting PPL increase $d_h(b)$ on a calibration set of 64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train.
This yields a distortion table of $H \times |\mathcal{B}|$ entries that serves as input to the solver.

The optimization in Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective} relies on an additive distortion assumption: the total PPL degradation from a mixed-precision allocation is approximately $\sum_h d_h(b_h)$.
This holds when per-head distortions are small and independent---a reasonable approximation for 4-bit and 8-bit quantization, where individual head distortions are typically below 0.1 PPL.
At 2-bit, however, individual distortions are orders of magnitude larger, and the additive assumption breaks down.

\subsection{Compounding Effect}
\label{sec:compounding}

When many heads are simultaneously quantized to 2-bit, per-head distortions compound non-additively.
The mechanism is straightforward: each head's quantized output feeds into the residual stream, and truncation errors from multiple 2-bit heads accumulate through subsequent layers.
When the number of 2-bit heads is small, these errors are absorbed by the remaining high-precision heads.
As the count grows, cumulative errors exceed the capacity of the residual stream to compensate, and PPL degrades super-linearly.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_compounding_curve.pdf}
\caption{PPL on Qwen2.5-7B ($4\times$ compression) as a function of $k$, the maximum number of 2-bit heads. Too few 2-bit heads waste budget on 4-bit; too many trigger compounding. The minimum occurs at $k{=}8$.}
\label{fig:compounding}
\end{figure}

Unconstrained solvers are blind to this effect because the additive objective underestimates the cost of large-scale 2-bit assignment.
On Qwen2.5-7B, unconstrained greedy assigns 68 heads to 2-bit and achieves 32.45 PPL; unconstrained MCKP assigns 75 heads and achieves 36.92---both far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Standard-resolution profiling detects non-zero $d_h(2)$ for only 37 of 112 heads; the remaining 75 heads have $d_h(2) \approx 0$, so most 2-bit assignments appear free to the additive objective.
The resulting additive prediction is $\sum_h d_h(b_h) + \text{baseline} \approx 11$ PPL---$3\text{--}4\times$ lower than the actual 32--37 PPL, because the compounding interaction between simultaneously quantized heads is invisible to per-head profiling.

This compounding is specific to 2-bit quantization.
At 4-bit and above, per-head distortions are small enough that additivity holds even when all heads share the same bit-width (uniform 4-bit achieves 15.45 PPL, close to the sum-of-distortions prediction).
The qualitative difference arises because 2-bit quantization has far larger per-head distortion, saturating the error tolerance of the residual stream.

Figure~\ref{fig:compounding} shows the relationship between $k$ (the maximum number of 2-bit heads) and PPL on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression.
The curve is U-shaped: at $k{=}0$ (uniform 4-bit), PPL is 15.45; allowing a few 2-bit heads reduces PPL by freeing budget for 8-bit heads on sensitive positions, reaching a minimum of 11.23 at $k{=}8$; beyond this point, compounding drives PPL upward, reaching 35.35 at $k{=}75$.

\subsection{Cardinality Constraint}
\label{sec:cardinality}

The compounding effect motivates a simple addition to Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective}: a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments.
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:constraint}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathbb{1}[b_h = 2] \leq k.
\end{equation}

The constraint parameter $k$ is selected by a small-scale sweep on calibration data: solve the constrained problem for each candidate $k$, evaluate calibration PPL, and pick the value at the minimum of the U-shaped curve (Figure~\ref{fig:compounding}).
For Qwen2.5-7B with 112 KV heads, $k{=}8$ ($\sim$7\% of heads).

The constraint is a single linear inequality, compatible with any solver---greedy, MCKP, or integer linear programming---and adds negligible overhead to the optimization.

A natural question is whether Layer-0 heads require explicit protection, since attention heads in the first layer are known to carry disproportionate importance.
On Qwen2.5-7B, the profiler assigns very high distortion to Layer-0 heads at 2-bit: L0H0 increases PPL by 31.9\% relative to the bf16 baseline (9.81 $\to$ 12.94), L0H2 by 23.2\% (9.81 $\to$ 12.09), L0H3 by 11.7\% (9.81 $\to$ 10.96).
These values are large enough that no solver would assign 2-bit to Layer-0 under any reasonable budget.
We verify this empirically: running the solver with and without manual Layer-0 exclusion produces identical allocations across all 112 heads.
No manual exclusion rule is needed; the profiler signal is sufficient.

\paragraph{Restoring additivity.}
The cardinality constraint resolves a tension between the profiling methodology (\S\ref{sec:profiling}) and the compounding effect (\S\ref{sec:compounding}): the additive objective in Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective} treats per-head distortions as independent, but 2-bit compounding violates this assumption once many 2-bit heads coexist.
Restricting the number of 2-bit heads to $k \ll H$ pushes the allocation back into a near-additive regime, where interactions between simultaneously quantized 2-bit heads are small enough that the profiler's additive prediction agrees with measured PPL.
For Qwen2.5-7B, $k{=}8$ corresponds to $\sim$7\% of the 112 heads---few enough that compounding contributes negligibly.
This is consistent with the U-shaped curve in Figure~\ref{fig:compounding}: the minimum at $k{=}8$ lies in the interval where the additive assumption is still a reasonable approximation, before compounding inflates true PPL above the additive prediction.
It also explains the gap between constrained and unconstrained solvers in Table~\ref{tab:solver_equiv}: constrained greedy operates inside the additive regime and attains 11.23 PPL, matching the additive estimate $\sum_h d_h(b_h) + \text{baseline} \approx 11$; unconstrained solvers extrapolate the same additive model outside its valid range and miss true PPL by $3\text{--}4\times$ (32.45 for greedy and 36.92 for MCKP, against the $\approx$11 they would predict).

\paragraph{Empirical observation.}
When the cardinality budget satisfies $k \ll H$ and the top-$k$ heads ranked by marginal benefit $d_h(4) - d_h(2)$ contain no ties, constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical per-head allocations.
We verify this across three architectures (Qwen2.5-7B: 112/112, Llama-3.1-8B: 256/256, Mistral-7B-v0.3: 255/256 heads identical; see per-head verification below).
Intuitively, the constraint restricts the feasible set to a small combinatorial space in which the only decision is which $k$ heads to assign 2-bit; the marginal-benefit ordering determines this set uniquely up to ties, so greedy's local choice coincides with the MCKP global optimum.

We verify this at the per-head level across three models:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Qwen2.5-7B:} 112/112 heads receive identical bit-widths.
\item \textbf{Llama-3.1-8B:} 256/256 heads identical.
\item \textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3:} 255/256 heads identical. The single difference is a zero-distortion tie between two heads at 4-bit and 8-bit, with no PPL impact.
\end{itemize}

The constraint narrows the feasible set enough that greedy's locally optimal decisions are globally optimal.
Without it, greedy cascades into excessive 2-bit allocation: each additional 2-bit head looks locally beneficial (freeing budget) but contributes to the compounding effect that degrades global PPL.
The cardinality constraint breaks this cascade by capping the number of 2-bit heads, aligning local and global optima.

The practical implication is that practitioners can use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm instead of MCKP without sacrificing optimality.

To verify that constrained MCKP is near-optimal, we perform a per-layer brute-force oracle on Qwen2.5-7B: for each of the 28 layers, we enumerate all $4^4{=}256$ bit-width assignments to the 4 KV heads and select the allocation minimizing per-layer PPL.
Of the 8 layers with non-trivial (non-all-4-bit) allocations, MCKP matches the oracle on 5; the remaining 3 have a maximum gap of 0.018 PPL---0.4\% of the constrained-vs-uniform improvement (4.53 PPL)---due to within-layer 2-bit head position swaps with no change to the per-layer bit budget.
Combined with the greedy--MCKP equivalence above, this closes the optimality chain: a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm (runtime 0.005s) produces allocations within 0.02 PPL of the brute-force optimum.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the objective's additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors are large enough to compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL for these allocations; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher.
At 4-bit and above, per-head distortions are small and compound negligibly---uniform 4-bit achieves close to its additive prediction---but 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger.
When most heads are quantized to 2-bit simultaneously, cumulative truncation errors exceed the network's capacity to compensate, and perplexity degrades super-linearly.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.

A surprising consequence is that, under the cardinality constraint, the choice of solver becomes irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical allocations---not approximately, but exactly: all 112 heads receive the same bit-width on Qwen2.5-7B, all 256 on Llama-3.1-8B, and 255 of 256 on Mistral-7B-v0.3 (the single difference is a zero-distortion tie with no PPL impact).
The constraint narrows the feasible set enough that greedy's locally optimal decisions are globally optimal (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm without sacrificing solution quality.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap across 28 layers is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On Llama-3.1-8B, constrained MCKP achieves 8.45 PPL vs.\ uniform 8.47---essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
On Mistral-7B-v0.3, it is slightly \emph{worse}: 7.16 vs.\ 7.13.
On Yi-1.5-9B, non-uniform allocation provides no benefit (7.22 vs.\ 7.22 uniform) despite Yi-1.5 having the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1).
On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1, the lowest ratio tested), degradation is 0.3\% (9.05 vs.\ 9.03).
The difference across architectures traces to head sensitivity heterogeneity---specifically, its \emph{distribution shape}, not GQA ratio alone.
Qwen's KV heads vary widely in 2-bit distortion, with Layer-0 heads forming a cluster of high sensitivity; Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier but otherwise uniform heads (a ``spike'' pattern that MCKP cannot exploit); Gemma-2 and Mistral show near-uniform sensitivity across all heads.
When there is no exploitable heterogeneity, non-uniform allocation adds noise without benefit.

This motivates a diagnostic question that prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint heterogeneity diagnostic based on concentration \emph{and} distribution shape of per-head distortion (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
On our five architectures, the diagnostic separates the beneficial case (Qwen, concentration 0.61, spread pattern) from cases where non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen's, but its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike with no cross-bitwidth gradient---precisely the pattern where MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
The diagnostic reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no computational overhead.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint makes solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent per-head allocations across three architectures, enabling use of a simple greedy algorithm (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates architectures where non-uniform allocation helps from those where it does not, across all five models tested. Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

To verify that the profiled allocation is not overfit to the calibration corpus, we profile on C4 and evaluate on WikiText-2, and vice versa, at $4\times$ compression.

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
4	A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
5	Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
6	The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
7	Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
8	Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
9	A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
10	This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.
11	
12	\paragraph{Limitations.}
13	Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
14	First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
15	Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
16	Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
17	Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
18	Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).
19	
20	\paragraph{Future Work.}
21	Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
22	Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.
23

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

input.old_string:
Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache promises lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width, but on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$, existing solvers fail catastrophically: unconstrained greedy and MCKP allocation achieve 32.45 and 36.92 perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B---far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
We trace this failure to \emph{2-bit distortion compounding}: when the majority of heads are assigned 2-bit precision, per-head quantization errors interact non-additively through the residual stream, violating the additive objective assumed by standard solvers.
We show that a single cardinality constraint capping the number of 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, constrained allocation achieves 11.23 perplexity, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint also renders solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent bit-width assignments across all three tested architectures ($\Delta{=}0.0000$), enabling use of a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm; per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality (max gap 0.02 PPL).
However, the benefit depends on architecture: on Llama-3.1-8B the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47), and on Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Notably, Yi-1.5-9B has the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1) and the highest top-5\% concentration (0.71), yet gains nothing from non-uniform allocation---because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, rather than the ``spread'' pattern that enables MCKP to redistribute budget across heads.
We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly identifies all five architectures studied---distinguishing spread heterogeneity (MCKP-exploitable) from spike and flat patterns where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.

Non-uniform per-head KV cache quantization helps only when head sensitivity exhibits a specific distribution shape---a finding obscured by prior work's focus on aggregate metrics.
We study five 7--9B architectures on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ and find that the benefit of per-head allocation depends not on GQA ratio or overall sensitivity magnitude, but on whether heterogeneity is \emph{spread} across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth gradients or concentrated in a single outlier.
On the one spread-pattern model (Qwen2.5-7B), a cardinality-constrained solver achieves 11.23 perplexity at $4\times$ compression---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45)---while unconstrained solvers fail catastrophically (32--37 PPL) due to 2-bit distortion compounding through the residual stream.

The cardinality constraint renders solver choice irrelevant---constrained greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations across all tested architectures---enabling a simple $O(H\log H)$ greedy algorithm.
We propose a joint empirical decision rule combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial ones across all five models studied.
